explanations: terra: After expulsion from the garden, earth becomes مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَىٰ حِينٍ; lost dwelling is answered by a measured new settlement and provision.
terra: Those who follow divine guidance are promised no fear and no grief, pairing the section's guidance root with the security that the city image seeks.
terra: A covenant forbids shedding one another's blood or expelling one another from homes, directly defining residence as protected by pact; 2:85 records its violation.
terra: The covenant people nevertheless kill and expel a group from their homes, then ransom captives, exposing the contradiction between pact and making residents unprotected.

luna: The section's Meccan sanctuary is a place of protection; this ayah condemns those who bar God's mosques and seek their ruin, saying their entry is only in fear, the reverse of a safe sacred place.

luna: The section's city is a bounded place of gathering and safety; this ayah calls the House a place of return for people and a place of security, making the sanctuary a shared civic center. | terra: God makes the House مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ وَأَمْنًا and charges Abraham and Ishmael to prepare it for worshippers, showing a place constituted as both return and security.

luna: The section cites Abraham's request for this balad to be safe and provisioned; this ayah joins safety and fruit to a limit on the disbeliever's enjoyment and a final fire, showing the city's abundance as a tested gift. | terra: Abraham asks that the settlement be secure and provisioned, while God's answer extends brief provision even to the unbeliever before fire; this ayah joins the section's city, food, faith, and opposite abode.

luna: The section describes the city as shaped by those who dwell there and cites a prayer for its safety in 2:126; this ayah shows Abraham and Ishmael raising the House's foundations, making the sanctuary's human construction part of that place. | terra: Abraham and Ishmael raise the House's foundations and ask acceptance, a concrete instance of inhabitants shaping the sacred place described in 2:125-126.

luna: The section names q-r-b both in the orphan's kinship and in dictionary form qurbān; this ayah joins close relatives, orphans and the needy as recipients of wealth, showing social nearness beside an offering's nearness to God.
luna: The section treats the city's sacred boundary and a truce as limits on exposure; this ayah forbids transgression in fighting, and 2:191 applies the limit specifically at the Sacred Mosque.

luna: The section says the same word-family can place a person outside the sanctuary's protection; this ayah forbids fighting at the Sacred Mosque unless the other side fights there, defining the boundary of its safety. | terra: Fighting is forbidden at the Sacred Mosque until aggression occurs there, and expulsion is answered in kind; the ayah marks the sanctuary's protection and the boundary at which it is violated.
luna: The section develops a truce between enemies; following 2:191's conditional fighting at the Sacred Mosque, this ayah says that if the other side stops, God is forgiving and merciful.

luna: The section's truce sense of q-s-m meets this limit on conflict: after the call to fight until persecution ends, this ayah says there is no aggression if the other side stops, except against wrongdoers.

luna: The section treats a sanctuary as a protected boundary; this ayah says sacred months and things have reciprocal limits and answers transgression only in equal measure. | terra: The sacred month and sacred things are subject to measured retaliation, defining inviolability through the boundary and proportion of its permitted breach.

luna: The section's dictionary forms B004-B005 pair al-hady with its maḥill; this ayah makes shaving wait until the offering reaches its place, so arrival at that place governs the rite. | terra: The command waits حَتَّىٰ يَبْلُغَ الْهَدْيُ مَحِلَّهُ, exactly staging the sacrificial animal travelling until it reaches its appointed place.

luna: The section develops the difference between protection inside the sanctuary and exposure outside it; this ayah calls fighting in a sacred month grave but also names barring people from the Sacred Mosque and expelling them, exposing violations of that boundary. | terra: Barring God's path and the Sacred Mosque and expelling its people are named together as grave offenses, making sanctuary include both access and inhabitants' right to remain.

luna: The section's Meccan balad is named here as Bakkah: the first House for humanity, blessed and guidance for all, locating the sanctuary within a wider human gathering. | terra: The first House established for humankind is at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for all peoples; it joins the city's sacred center to the section's guidance root.

luna: The section presents the city as a place of protection; this ayah says whoever enters the House is safe and makes pilgrimage there a duty, joining safety to arrival. | terra: وَمَن دَخَلَهُ كَانَ آمِنًا makes entry into the House's precinct an entry into protection, the clearest Quranic realization of a secure lodging.
terra: قُرْبَانٍ تَأْكُلُهُ النَّارُ names an offering consumed by fire, a direct Quranic scene for the dictionary sense attached to the section's قرب root.

luna: The section makes the city a possible place of shelter; the oppressed here ask to be brought out of a town whose people are wrongdoers and for a protecting ally, showing the reverse of a safe abode. | terra: Oppressed residents ask to be brought out of هَٰذِهِ الْقَرْيَةِ الظَّالِمِ أَهْلُهَا and given a protector and helper, defining a city by inhabitants who have made dwelling unsafe.
terra: People joined to a treaty community, or those who withdraw and offer peace, are protected from attack; refuge, pact, and restraint from fighting meet explicitly.
terra: Those seeking safety from both sides lose that protection if they neither withdraw nor offer peace, showing the covenant boundary by its failure and continuing 4:90.
terra: Those who remain oppressed are asked whether God's earth was spacious enough to emigrate, placing unsafe residence against available departure; 4:98 names those unable to make that move.
terra: Powerless men, women, and children who can neither devise a plan nor find a way are excepted from the migration demand of 4:97, identifying those genuinely trapped in an unsafe place.
terra: The emigrant in God's cause is promised many places of refuge and abundance on earth, directly opposing forced departure with new protected and provisioned places.
terra: The ayah commands fulfillment of covenants, makes livestock lawful, and withholds hunting while consecrated; pact, offering-animal, and the root's lawful/sacred boundary converge.

luna: The section's root ح ل ل has two stated faces: violating sacred things and leaving ihram; this ayah forbids violating the sacred signs and hady, then permits hunting once people have left the sacred state. | terra: لَا تُحِلُّوا protects God's rites, sacred month, and الْهَدْيَ, while وَإِذَا حَلَلْتُمْ permits hunting after consecration; one ayah displays the root's opposed sanctuary senses.

luna: The section defines dictionary form qurbān as an offering brought near to God; the sons of Adam each present a قُرْبَانًا, and the ayah distinguishes the offering accepted by God from the one rejected. | terra: The two sons of Adam each offer قُرْبَانًا and acceptance distinguishes them, directly realizing the source dictionary's thing brought near to God.

luna: The section explores the boundary between the sacred state and release from it; this ayah tests believers with game within reach while they are in that state, giving the boundary a concrete restraint on taking.

luna: The section's hady is an offering carried to its place; this ayah requires a replacement offering هَدْيًا بَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ for a hunting violation in the sacred state, tying sanctuary boundaries to sacrifice. | terra: The penalty for hunting in consecration is هَدْيًا بَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ, another exact scene of an offering defined by reaching the sanctuary.

luna: The section notes that ح ل ل can name release from a sacred limit; this ayah contrasts permitted sea game and food for travelers with forbidden land game while in ihram, making the boundary govern provision. | terra: Sea game is permitted while land game is forbidden as long as people remain in consecration, clarifying the legal boundary between حِلّ and حَرَم around the sanctuary journey.

luna: The section makes the city a scene of safety and provision; this ayah says God made the Kaaba a support for people, alongside the sacred month and offerings, so the House sustains communal life. | terra: The Kaaba, sacred month, sacrificial animals, and garlands are all appointed as supports for people, joining sacred place, protected time, and the offering headed there.
terra: For faith unconfused by wrongdoing, لَهُمُ الْأَمْنُ وَهُم مُّهْتَدُونَ brings together the section's named roots of security and guidance as one condition.
luna: The section centers a city and its people; this ayah describes a blessed Book sent to warn the Mother of Cities and those around it, extending the city's relation to its surrounding region.
terra: Believers have دَارُ السَّلَامِ with their Lord, who is their protecting ally, uniting secure abode and protection as the positive destination.
terra: The declaration that prayer, sacrifice, life, and death belong to God states the consecrating stance behind the dictionary's offering brought near to Him.
terra: Many towns receive divine punishment by night or during midday rest, placing catastrophe precisely within the rhythms of inhabited settlement.
terra: God establishes humankind on earth and places livelihoods there, expressing the section's link between being made resident and being provisioned.
terra: The repeated descent scene gives humankind on earth مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَىٰ حِينٍ, joining relocation, residence, and temporary sustenance.
terra: Rain is driven to بَلَدٍ مَّيِّتٍ and brings forth fruit, using the section's city root for lifeless land whose capacity to sustain inhabitants is restored; 7:58 contrasts kinds of land.
terra: الْبَلَدُ الطَّيِّبُ yields vegetation while bad land yields little, making the quality of the place legible in its provision and completing 7:57's revived-land scene.

luna: The section defines the city as a bounded place shaped by residents and their staying; this ayah says Thamud were settled in the land and made palaces on its plains and houses in its mountains, showing people forming their inhabited landscape.

luna: The section says a city's residents shape its condition; this ayah says towns would have received blessings from heaven and earth had their people believed, but denial brought seizure. | terra: Had the people of the towns believed, blessings would have opened from heaven and earth; their denial brings seizure instead, making residents' faith determine whether their place is fed or punished.

luna: The section makes the city a scene of safety; this ayah asks whether town-dwellers felt secure from God's punishment arriving by night while they slept. | terra: The people of towns feel secure while divine might can come by night as they sleep, setting inhabited repose against punishment alighting without warning.

luna: The section makes a city a sheltering place; this adjacent ayah asks whether its people felt secure from punishment arriving by day while they played. | terra: The people of towns feel secure while punishment can come in daylight during play, completing the day-and-night boundary around false urban safety.

luna: The section holds urban security beside the possibility of punishment; this ayah closes the questions in 7:97-98 by asking whether the town-dwellers felt safe from God's plan. | terra: The rhetorical question denies that anyone can be secure from God's plan, qualifying every claim of safety attached to a place.

luna: The section cites fear that following guidance could mean being snatched from one's land, answered by a secure sanctuary; this ayah recalls believers fearing people would snatch them from the land until God gave them shelter, help and provision.
terra: The unbelievers plot to detain, kill, or expel the Messenger, exposing the man addressed in the city as one denied ordinary protection.

luna: The section's sanctuary is a place of protection; this ayah says disbelievers bar people from the Sacred Mosque and denies that they are its guardians, reversing the idea that mere presence confers its protection. | terra: Those who bar access to the Sacred Mosque are denied its guardianship; the ayah separates mere control by inhabitants from the piety that warrants protection of the place.

luna: The section says residents shape the city they inhabit; this adjacent ayah describes the disbelievers' conduct at the House as whistling and clapping and links it to punishment, showing a sanctuary dishonored by its occupants.

luna: The section's root note B008 gives q-s-m the dictionary sense of a truce between enemies; this ayah says that if the enemy inclines to peace, the believers should incline to it, stating the truce's reciprocal action. | terra: If the enemy inclines to peace, the Messenger must incline to it and trust God, giving the truce sense named under the section's oath root a direct Quranic stance.
terra: This ayah joins those who emigrated with those who gave shelter and aid, then limits aid where a treaty مِيثَاق stands; migration, refuge, and pact meet in one legal scene.
terra: Those who emigrate and those who shelter and aid them are called true believers and promised forgiveness and generous provision, adding sustenance to the refuge scene stated in 8:72.

luna: The section names an ahd as what protects a person; this ayah commands that treaties with polytheists who kept them be completed to their term, clarifying how protection lasts by a kept covenant. | terra: Treaties with polytheists who have kept every term must be fulfilled to their end, a direct formulation of the source dictionary's truce and of protection bounded by covenant.

luna: The section's dictionary form hadī (B007) is a person who comes to a group seeking protection; here a polytheist who asks for protection is granted it and escorted to a safe place, making refuge a concrete duty. | terra: A hostile outsider who asks protection must be sheltered and then conveyed to مَأْمَنَهُ; this enacts the source dictionary's protected stranger and secure lodging against the unprotected man.

luna: The section names a truce between enemies and Muslims and a person with or without an ahd; this ayah specifies a covenant made at the Sacred Mosque and commands reciprocal fidelity while the other party keeps it. | terra: A treaty made with polytheists عِندَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ must be honored while they honor it, directly locating pact and mutual protection at the sanctuary.
terra: The aggressors respect neither bond nor covenant toward a believer, closely realizing the source dictionary's exposed person who has no عهد or حرمة.
terra: Breaking oaths after covenant makes the offenders leaders of disbelief to be opposed; it directly joins oath and failed truce, and 9:13 adds their attempt to expel the Messenger.
terra: The offenders broke their oaths and intended إِخْرَاجِ الرَّسُولِ, joining the section's truce sense with the threatened removal of the addressed man from his place.

luna: The section treats a sacred place as shaped by those who inhabit and guard it; this ayah disqualifies polytheists from maintaining God's mosques, while 9:18 names the believers who may maintain them.

luna: The section says a city takes its character from its residents; this ayah gives maintenance of God's mosques to those who believe, pray, give charity and fear God, specifying the community that tends the sacred place.

luna: The section joins sanctuary, visitors and provision; this ayah names watering pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque, then distinguishes those services from belief and striving, adding the work that sustains a pilgrimage center.

luna: The section joins a sacred city's boundary to its provision; this ayah bars polytheists from the Sacred Mosque, then answers fear of poverty with God's promise of enrichment, setting exclusion beside provision. | terra: Polytheists are barred from approaching the Sacred Mosque, while fear of poverty is answered with promised divine enrichment, joining sanctuary boundary and provision.
terra: When the unbelievers expel the Messenger, God protects him as one of two in the cave; forced departure from the city becomes a scene of divine refuge.

luna: The section's root note B002 connects miskin with dwelling; this ayah promises believers good dwellings in the Gardens of Eden, giving the word-family a lasting abode as well as an earthly one. | terra: God promises believers good dwellings in gardens of lasting residence, another explicit pairing of faith with a protected enduring home.

luna: The section defines qurbān as what is brought near to God; this ayah calls spending قُرُبَاتٍ عِندَ اللَّهِ, explicitly treating material giving as a means of nearness. | terra: Some spending is taken as قُرُبَاتٍ عِندَ اللَّهِ and a means to the Messenger's prayers, confirming that what brings near can be expenditure rather than an animal offering.
terra: God calls to دَارِ السَّلَامِ and guides whom He wills to a straight path, directly joining the secure home to the section's guidance root.
terra: God guarantees every creature's provision and knows مُسْتَقَرَّهَا وَمُسْتَوْدَعَهَا, placing sustenance beside its settled and entrusted locations.
terra: وَيَحِلُّ عَلَيْهِ عَذَابٌ مُّقِيمٌ makes punishment both something that alights and something that remains, fusing the section's descent and residence senses.
terra: The blast overtakes the wrongdoers and leaves them lifeless in their homes, another exact meeting of settled houses and punishment arriving; 11:68 describes the erasure of their residence.
terra: Thamud are said to be as though they had never dwelt there, making the inhabitants' disappearance undo the place itself after the blast of 11:67.

luna: The section says residents shape the city they inhabit; this ayah says God would not destroy towns unjustly while their people were reforming, tying a town's fate to its residents' conduct. | terra: God does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are reformers, directly making a settlement's fate answer to the conduct of those who inhabit it.

luna: The section makes a city an arrival point where a person may be safe; Joseph tells his family to enter Egypt safely, a separate scene of secure entry into a settled land. | terra: Joseph says ادْخُلُوا مِصْرَ ... آمِنِينَ, staging entry into an inhabited land as arrival into safety.

luna: The section's dictionary sense B004 of ح ل ل is that punishment descends; this ayah says a calamity may come near the disbelievers' homes, bringing that root's downward arrival into the city-and-dwelling scene. | terra: A calamity may تَحُلُّ قَرِيبًا مِّن دَارِهِمْ, using the same verb for an affliction alighting near the unbelievers' dwelling.

luna: The section's dictionary sense B004 is punishment coming down; this adjacent ayah adds that earlier messengers were mocked and the deniers were eventually seized, completing 13:31's warning of calamity near their homes.

luna: The section's dictionary sense B002 of ح ل ل is settling in an abode; this ayah says wrongdoers settled their people in the house of ruin, reversing the secure dwelling. | terra: Those who exchange God's favor for unbelief وَأَحَلُّوا قَوْمَهُمْ دَارَ الْبَوَارِ, making leaders place their people in the ruinous opposite of a secure city.

luna: The section contrasts settling in a permanent home with destructive settlement; following 14:28's house of ruin, this ayah identifies that destination as Hell, showing the consequence of the placement. | terra: This ayah identifies the preceding دَارَ الْبَوَارِ as Hell and calls it بِئْسَ الْقَرَارُ; its own contribution is the character of that destination as the worst settlement.

luna: The section's balad is a settled city whose residents give it its character; Abraham asks that this very balad be made safe, grounding the civic image in a prayer for protection. | terra: Abraham asks رَبِّ اجْعَلْ هَٰذَا الْبَلَدَ آمِنًا; the city, its safety, and a prayer for that safety are the direct counterpart to the section's inhabited and protected place.

luna: The section says a city's ability to house people depends on provision; Abraham says he settled some descendants in a barren valley by the sacred House and asks for hearts to incline and fruit to reach them. | terra: Abraham says أَسْكَنْتُ مِن ذُرِّيَّتِي in a barren valley beside the inviolable House and asks that produce reach them, directly joining settlement, sanctuary, and the food that makes dwelling possible.

luna: The section's root note B002 glosses س ك ن as dwelling in a house; this ayah says people settled in the homes of those who wronged themselves and saw what befell them, making a dwelling both shelter and a warning from its former residents.
terra: The God-fearing are amid gardens and springs, supplying the provisioned setting into which 15:46 tells them to enter safely.
terra: ادْخُلُوهَا بِسَلَامٍ آمِنِينَ makes the final garden a protected place entered and inhabited, extending the city's security to the lasting abode.

luna: The section presents the city as a place of security and habitation; this ayah says the people carved secure houses in the mountains, while 15:83 completes the scene with a sudden blast. | terra: Thamud carve mountain houses آمِنِينَ, a humanly fortified residence whose security is overturned by the cry in 15:83.

luna: The section's secure-city scene has a contrary end when punishment arrives; after 15:82's secure carved homes, this ayah says a blast seized their people in the morning. | terra: The blast takes the secure house-builders at morning, contributing the descending catastrophe that exposes the limit of the safety claimed in 15:82.
terra: Pack animals carry burdens to a بَلَد that people could scarcely reach unaided, presenting a town as a journey's destination and echoing the offering that walks until its appointed place.
terra: Those who emigrate after being wronged are promised a good lodging in this world, replacing forced movement with a divinely provided place.

luna: The section's root note for miskin links س ك ن to dwelling; this ayah says God made homes a place of rest and also made portable shelters, connecting settling to the shelter that lets people remain. | terra: God makes houses سَكَنًا and tents light both when travelling and when stopping, directly setting settled home beside departure and temporary encampment.
terra: God supplies shade, mountain shelters, and protective clothing, extending the houses and travel tents of 16:80 into the means that make a place habitable and safe.
terra: The command to fulfill God's covenant and not break confirmed oaths is a direct Quranic formulation of oath functioning as a protected pact.
terra: Those who emigrate after persecution, then strive and endure, receive divine forgiveness and mercy, making forced displacement a passage into protection.

luna: The section pictures the city as sheltered and well-provisioned; this ayah's town is initially secure and supplied from every place, then disbelief turns that condition into hunger and fear. | terra: A town once secure and tranquil with abundant provision becomes clothed in hunger and fear for ingratitude, the exact reversal of the section's protected and fed city.

luna: The section says a city is affected by the people who settle in it and names punishment that descends; this ayah says a town's affluent residents disobeyed before it was destroyed, making the inhabitants' conduct the cause of the reversal. | terra: A town's affluent inhabitants transgress and the sentence falls on the town, joining resident-shaped place with punishment becoming due.

luna: The section opens with the Messenger present in the city; this ayah says his opponents nearly drove him from the land, placing his stay in the city beside the threat of expulsion. | terra: The addressee is nearly uprooted from the land so as to be expelled, after which his expellers would remain only briefly; residence and removal directly turn on his presence.
terra: The sheltered youths send one companion cautiously into the city to buy wholesome food, joining refuge, urban provision, and the danger of discovery; 18:20 states that danger.
terra: If the city's people discover the youths, they will stone them or force them back into their creed, revealing the provision-bearing city of 18:19 as unsafe for the outsiders.
terra: The towns are destroyed when their inhabitants do wrong, with an appointed time for destruction, again locating a place's fate in its residents and a measured arrival.
terra: Two travellers ask a town's people for food and are refused hospitality, making the moral character of the place visible through how its residents receive unprovided strangers.

luna: The section's dictionary sense B004 of ح ل ل is that punishment descends; this ayah warns that God's anger may come down on those who transgress and says the one it reaches has fallen, turning a settled community's security into exposure. | terra: فَيَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبِي uses the section's named sense of wrath descending and becoming due, and the one upon whom it descends then falls.
terra: Adam is warned that the enemy may expel him and his wife from the garden and make him suffer, a direct loss-of-dwelling scene whose material security is detailed in 20:118-119.
terra: The garden's dwelling guarantees neither hunger nor nakedness, making residence inseparable from provision and shelter; 20:117 supplies the threat of expulsion.
terra: The garden also guarantees neither thirst nor exposure to the sun, completing the protected, provisioned home described in 20:117-118.

luna: The section defines the city through those who reside there; this ayah makes residents and visitors from afar equal at the Sacred Mosque, while condemning those who bar access, showing how a sacred place gathers people and sets a boundary. | terra: At the Sacred Mosque the resident الْعَاكِفُ and the visitor الْبَادِ are made equal, while attempted violation receives punishment; the ayah defines the sanctuary through residence, access, and a protected boundary.

luna: The section describes place as bounded and shaped by its inhabitants; this ayah says God established the place of the House for Abraham and commands its purification, grounding the boundary in a deliberate act. | terra: God assigns Abraham the site of the House and commands him to purify it for worshippers, showing sacred place being prepared through human residence and service; 22:27 brings people to it.

luna: The section says a city gathers those who settle and arrive; this ayah calls people to pilgrimage and depicts them arriving on foot and by camel from distant passes. | terra: Pilgrims come on foot and lean mounts from every distant pass, a direct arrival scene at the sacred destination whose rites and offerings continue in 22:28-33.

luna: The section joins hady, provision and the miskin; this ayah has pilgrims mention God over livestock He provided and feed the distressed poor, linking offerings to sustenance for the vulnerable. | terra: Pilgrims name God over provided livestock, then eat and feed the destitute, linking the journey to the House, sacrificial provision, and the poor person's food.

luna: The section places the offering at the Ancient House; after the pilgrimage rites in 22:28, this ayah adds fulfilling vows and circumambulating the House, showing what arrival at that place completes. | terra: Pilgrims complete their rites, fulfill vows, and circle the Ancient House, locating the vowed act at the destination reached in the surrounding pilgrimage passage.
terra: Honoring God's sacred limits is declared good, while livestock is made lawful except for stated prohibitions; it continues the sanctuary passage through the lawful-inviolable boundary.

luna: The section links the sanctuary and sacrificial signs to the approach to God; this ayah says honoring God's rites comes from hearts' piety, clarifying the inward reverence that gives those visible boundaries meaning. | terra: Honoring God's sacrificial signs is traced to piety of hearts, supplying the inward protection of the rites whose destination is named in 22:33.

luna: The section's dictionary form maḥill is the destination of hady; this ayah says the animals' final place is the Ancient House, directly placing the offering at its destination. | terra: ثُمَّ مَحِلُّهَا إِلَى الْبَيْتِ الْعَتِيقِ explicitly gives sacrificial animals their appointed destination at the Ancient House.

luna: The section discusses hady and qurbān as offerings and provision; this ayah says every community has a rite for mentioning God over livestock He provided, placing the Meccan offering among a wider pattern of worship. | terra: Every community receives a rite for naming God over the livestock He provides, joining offering, divine provision, and worship.

luna: The section links a city to provision for the miskin; this ayah makes sacrificial camels a sign and commands people to eat from them and feed both the needy and the one who asks. | terra: Sacrificial camels are God's signs and, once laid down, feed both the contented and the asker, joining the offering at the sanctuary with provision for people in need.

luna: The section defines qurbān as what is brought near to God and traces hady to its physical place; this ayah says meat and blood do not reach God, but piety does, distinguishing arrival at the House from spiritual acceptance. | terra: Neither the sacrificial animals' flesh nor blood reaches God, but piety does; this distinguishes the offering's physical arrival at its place from what spiritually reaches God.

luna: The section describes a person without protection and another seeking refuge; this ayah gives the wronged permission to defend themselves, and 22:40 adds that they were expelled from homes and explains the protection of worship places.

luna: The section makes sanctuary a place of protection; this ayah says God repels some people by others so houses where His name is mentioned will not be demolished, showing what protection preserves. | terra: Those expelled unjustly from their homes are linked to God's protection of houses of worship from demolition, joining lost residence with the defense of sacred places.

luna: The section describes a city through its residents and their staying; this ayah recalls towns destroyed for wrongdoing, with abandoned wells and lofty palaces, showing settled places emptied by punishment. | terra: Destroyed wrongdoing towns leave collapsed roofs, abandoned wells, and lofty palaces, showing the built marks of settlement after inhabitants and protection are gone.

luna: The section joins a safe place to worship of its Lord; this promise says God will establish believers in the land and replace their fear with security so they may worship Him, making safety a condition of settled worship.
terra: The people of Paradise have the better مُسْتَقَرًّا and resting place, a positive counterpart to the ruinous and painful abodes developed by the section.
terra: Water revives بَلْدَةً مَّيْتًا and gives drink to animals and many people, linking the different 'dead land' sense of بلد to the section's fed human place.
terra: Hell is called سَاءَتْ مُسْتَقَرًّا وَمُقَامًا, the evil settled residence that illuminates the opposite endpoint from the secure abiding home.
terra: أَتُتْرَكُونَ فِي مَا هَاهُنَا آمِنِينَ questions whether Thamud can remain secure in place; 26:147-149 spell out the provision and houses meant by 'here.'
terra: Gardens and springs are part of the 'here' in which Thamud expects to remain secure in 26:146, contributing the provisioned landscape of the settlement.
terra: Fields and soft-clustered palms add cultivated food to the secure settlement of 26:146 before 26:149 names its carved houses.
terra: Thamud carve houses from the mountains, the resident-made built environment within the secure and provisioned place described in 26:146-148.

luna: The section's city is sacred and inhabited; the speaker says he was commanded to worship the Lord of this town, the One who made it sacred, joining the city's boundary to worship. | terra: The Messenger is commanded to worship the Lord of هَٰذِهِ الْبَلْدَةِ الَّذِي حَرَّمَهَا; the addressed person, the city, and its God-given inviolability coincide.
terra: A man comes from the far end of the city to warn Moses that the chiefs plan to kill him and tells him to leave, a parallel city scene of an unprotected man; 28:21 gives the flight.
terra: Moses leaves the city fearful and watchful, asking rescue from its wrongdoing people; 28:20 supplies the urban plot and 28:22 the guided journey that follows.
terra: After fleeing the city, Moses hopes his Lord will يَهْدِيَنِي سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ; the ayah links displacement to guidance toward a new destination, continuing 28:20-21.

luna: The section cites the fear of following guidance in 28:57; this preceding ayah says the Messenger cannot guide whom he loves but God guides whom He wills, framing the concern that the next ayah answers with a secure sanctuary.

luna: The section places security and fruit in one city; people fear that following guidance will get them snatched from their land, and the reply points to a secure sanctuary to which fruit is brought. | terra: The fear that following guidance will mean being snatched from one's land is answered with حَرَمًا آمِنًا to which every kind of fruit is brought, uniting guidance, protected residence, and provision.

luna: The section defines a town through its settled residents and its provision; this ayah says many towns grew insolent in their livelihood and their homes remained nearly uninhabited after them, reversing the nourished dwelling. | terra: Towns exulting in their livelihood are destroyed and their dwellings remain almost wholly uninhabited, reversing provisioned residence into an emptied place.
terra: God does not destroy towns until a messenger addresses their central town, and destruction follows only the inhabitants' wrongdoing; speaker and residents define the city's accountability.
terra: Night is made for repose and day for seeking God's bounty, connecting the root's rest sense with the alternating provision that supports settled life.

terra: The promise to return the addressee to مَعَادٍ can be read as return to Mecca after departure; that place-identification is interpretive, but it specifically answers the image of the Messenger placed in and expelled from the city.

terra: Believing servants are told that God's earth is spacious and to worship Him, so an unsafe dwelling need not imprison worship; this parallels worship of the Lord of the sacred city under threatened migration.
terra: Believers are lodged in elevated chambers of Paradise, a lasting replacement for insecure earthly residence in the migration passage beginning at 29:56.
terra: Creatures that do not carry their own provision are sustained by God along with people, answering the provision anxiety implicit in leaving one's place in 29:56.

luna: The section makes the city a protected place; this ayah asks whether people see that a secure sanctuary stands amid surrounding abduction, so its safety is a real boundary against danger. | terra: حَرَمًا آمِنًا is set against people being snatched away all around it, sharpening the section's boundary between protected sanctuary and exposed person.
terra: People claim their houses are exposed and seek permission to leave, though the ayah says they only intend flight; it tests the claimed boundary between unsafe home and departure.

luna: The section calls the city a place marked by its inhabitants and their staying; this ayah locates Saba's sign in their dwelling, with gardens, provision and a good town, showing settlement as nourished life. | terra: Saba's dwelling is a sign with gardens, the command to eat God's provision, and بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ, presenting a good town through the sustenance of its inhabitants.

luna: The section calls a city a place shaped by the life of its residents; this ayah says Saba turned away and a flood replaced their two gardens with bitter growth, turning a provision-rich dwelling into loss.
luna: The section sets a fed city beside its residents' conduct; following Saba's lost gardens in 34:16, this ayah names disbelief as the recompense, completing the reversal of provision.

luna: The section joins a settled town to safety and provision; this ayah describes blessed towns placed along a route and travel between them by night and day in safety. | terra: Visible settlements are set along Saba's route and they are told to travel among them nights and days آمِنِينَ, combining bounded towns, movement, and security.

luna: The section's image holds settlement beside movement between places; after 34:18's safe route between towns, this ayah says the people asked for longer distances between journeys and were scattered, reversing connected settlement into dispersal. | terra: After the safe, closely spaced journey of 34:18, the people ask for longer stages and are scattered, reversing connected secure settlements into dispersal.
terra: Clouds are driven to بَلَدٍ مَّيِّتٍ and the earth is revived, a different sense of the city root that marks the boundary between lifeless ground and a place able to host life.
luna: The section cites the lasting abode in 35:35; the preceding ayah says its people praise God for removing grief, completing the secure-home image with release from sorrow.

luna: The section's dictionary sense B002 of ح ل ل is settling in a place; this ayah says God settled the believers in the abode of permanence by His bounty, giving that verb family a lasting, secure destination. | terra: The people of Paradise praise the One who أَحَلَّنَا دَارَ الْمُقَامَةِ, the positive endpoint of being placed in an abiding home.
terra: Abraham tells his son of the command to sacrifice him, and the son consents, providing the intended sacrificial act whose ransom appears in 37:107.
terra: Father and son submit and the son is laid down for sacrifice, contributing the bodily placement at the heart of the offering scene resolved in 37:107.
terra: God ransoms Abraham's son with a great sacrifice, a direct sacrificial offering that resolves the submission and intended slaughter of 37:102-103.
terra: The repeated formula وَيَحِلُّ عَلَيْهِ عَذَابٌ مُّقِيمٌ again presents lasting punishment as an arrival that takes up residence.
terra: The inheritors of Paradise settle wherever they wish in its land, presenting the lasting reward as freely chosen residence.
terra: This near life is temporary enjoyment while the Hereafter is دَارُ الْقَرَارِ, drawing the boundary between a passing station and the lasting home.
terra: The fire is called the enemies' دَارُ الْخُلْدِ, another ruinous permanent home set against the secure abode.

luna: The section centers the city and its people; this ayah says the Arabic revelation warns the Mother of Cities and those around it, making the city a center whose warning reaches beyond its boundary.
terra: Measured water revives بَلْدَةً مَّيْتًا, making the land's habitability depend on provision that arrives by measure.
terra: The God-fearing are placed فِي مَقَامٍ أَمِينٍ, a secure station whose provisioned setting is supplied by 44:52.
terra: Gardens and springs furnish the secure station named in 44:51, so this ayah contributes the sustenance and setting of that protected abode.
terra: The stronger town is called قَرْيَتِكَ الَّتِي أَخْرَجَتْكَ, making the Messenger's own city an agent through its inhabitants' expulsion of him and then subject to destruction.

luna: The section places protection and lack of protection inside the city; this ayah says God restrained both sides' hands in the middle of Mecca, while 48:25 adds that the offering was held back from its place, showing restraint within the sanctuary conflict. | terra: God restrains both sides' hands in the valley of Mecca, creating protected space amid conflict; 48:25 then shows access to the sanctuary and the offering still blocked.
terra: The unbelievers bar the believers from the Sacred Mosque and hold الْهَدْيَ back from أَن يَبْلُغَ مَحِلَّهُ, showing the section's destination scene through its obstruction.

luna: The section gathers safety, hostility and truce in the Meccan sanctuary; this ayah contrasts the disbelievers' zeal with God's sending calm upon the Messenger and believers, continuing the restrained confrontation of 48:24-25. | terra: In the sanctuary conflict, unbelieving zeal is answered when God sends السَّكِينَةَ upon the Messenger and believers; this nearby ayah gives the dwelling root's tranquility sense to the people blocked in 48:25.

luna: The section connects the sanctuary, the offering's destination and release from ihram; this ayah promises entry into the Sacred Mosque safely, without fear, with heads shaved or shortened, reversing the blocked access of 48:25. | terra: The believers are promised entry into the Sacred Mosque آمِنِينَ, with the pilgrimage rites completed, presenting secure arrival at the sacred destination.
terra: Provision for servants revives بَلْدَةً مَّيْتًا; here the named root denotes lifeless land rather than an inhabited city, while sustenance turns it toward habitation.

terra: The People of the Book are expelled from their homes after believing their fortresses would protect them, and their own houses are ruined; built security, residence, and removal reverse together.
terra: Had God not decreed evacuation for them, worldly punishment would have come instead, while fire remains in the Hereafter; this ayah distinguishes exile from the two punitive abodes after 59:2.

luna: The section's dictionary form hadī describes someone seeking shelter with a group; this ayah describes poor emigrants driven from their homes and possessions, making the need for a receiving community concrete.

luna: The section's hadī is one who comes to a people for protection; this ayah describes the residents who made the abode and faith their own and loved those who migrated to them, showing shelter as a communal welcome. | terra: Those who تَبَوَّءُوا الدَّارَ وَالْإِيمَانَ receive and prefer the emigrants, turning settled residence into protection and provision for newcomers.
terra: The enemy expelled the Messenger and believers solely for faith, so the ayah joins the addressed man's forced departure with the boundary of protective friendship.

luna: The section names the truce as a relation between enemies and discusses who has protection; this ayah says kindness and justice remain permitted toward those who neither fight believers nor expel them from their homes, setting a boundary for peaceful relations. | terra: Those who neither fight believers over religion nor expel them from their homes may receive kindness and justice, defining peaceful protection by the absence of expulsion; 60:9 supplies the boundary.

luna: The section describes a person outside protection and a city that can shelter or expose its residents; this ayah names those who fought believers, expelled them from their homes, or helped expel them as the boundary for alliance. | terra: The forbidden allies are precisely those who fight, expel believers from their homes, or assist that expulsion, making loss of dwelling the line that ends peaceful relations in 60:8.

luna: The section's root note B002 links س ك ن to dwelling; this ayah promises good dwellings in the Gardens of Eden alongside salvation, repeating the enduring-home sense. | terra: Forgiveness is paired with gardens and pleasant dwellings in lasting gardens, repeating the positive endpoint of being placed in an abiding home.

terra: A faction boasts that the mightier will expel the lowlier from the city, while the ayah assigns might to God, the Messenger, and believers; civic power is exposed as a claim over who may remain.
terra: أَسْكِنُوهُنَّ مِنْ حَيْثُ سَكَنْتُم مِّن وُجْدِكُمْ explicitly ties another person's housing to the resident's means, supporting the section's claim that dwelling depends on provision.
terra: Each person is ordered to spend according to what God has given, supplying the means-based maintenance principle that continues the housing command in 65:6.
terra: God makes the earth manageable, commands people to walk its paths, and tells them to eat His provision, joining inhabitable ground, movement, and sustenance.
terra: The question asks whether people feel secure from the inhabited earth being made to swallow them, placing confidence in one's ground against sudden divine upheaval.
terra: The next question asks whether people feel secure from a stone-bearing storm, extending 67:16's boundary on place-based safety to punishment descending from above.

luna: The section's root note for miskin links it to dwelling and says provision makes dwelling possible; this ayah names the needy alongside the orphan and captive as people given food, showing the sustenance at stake in that dwelling.

luna: The section ties the miskin's ability to remain somewhere to provision; this ayah condemns people who do not urge one another to feed the needy, showing the failure to sustain the poor resident.

luna: The section cites this city as a place of safety; the oath names وَهَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ الْأَمِينِ, giving the city itself the quality Abraham prayed for elsewhere. | terra: The matching oath names the same place as وَهَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ الْأَمِينِ, making security the explicit quality of the city in which the addressee is placed.

terra: The elephant episode is traditionally the attempted attack on the Meccan sanctuary; on that contextual identification, the ayah recalls the Lord's protection of the city, though the ayah itself does not name the city or House.

luna: The section presents the city as a community formed by its inhabitants; this ayah names Quraysh, while 106:2-4 specify their seasonal journeys, the House, food and safety, identifying the community behind the city image. | terra: The bond or accustomed security of Quraysh identifies the resident people whose ordered life belongs to the House; 106:2 specifies the journeys sustaining that life and 106:3-4 its Lord, food, and safety.

luna: The section says city life depends on provision; this ayah names Quraysh's winter and summer journeys, while 106:3-4 connect the community to the House, food and security, showing movement behind the city's provision. | terra: The winter and summer caravans show the fed city's residence depending on regular departure and return, a concrete meeting of settlement, travel, and provision completed in 106:3-4.

luna: The section makes the populated city a place of shelter and provision; this ayah tells Quraysh to worship the Lord of this House, tying the community's life to its sanctuary. | terra: The command فَلْيَعْبُدُوا رَبَّ هَٰذَا الْبَيْتِ matches worship of the Lord who made the city sacred; 106:4 states what His lordship provides there.

luna: The section says that a city's ability to shelter people rests on provision; this ayah says the Lord of the House fed Quraysh against hunger and secured them from fear, joining sustenance and safety. | terra: The Lord of the House feeds against hunger and grants safety against fear, making explicit the section's claim that the sacred city stands as a fed and protected place; 106:3 identifies the House.

luna: The section links the miskin's ability to dwell to provision; this ayah condemns the one who will not urge feeding الْمِسْكِينِ, showing the social failure that leaves the needy without sustenance.
terra: The command to pray to the Lord and sacrifice gives a compressed speaker stance for the source dictionary's offering brought near to God.
